questions.q: Which baseline is best for a pure random walk?
why: Correct: the last value is the best forecast of a random walk.
The mean ignores the current level.
No season exists in a random walk.
Drift is for a steady trend. It adds noise if there is no drift.

questions.q: Daily data, weekly season (m = 7). The last 7 values are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. What is the seasonal naive forecast for h = 9?
questions.why: h = 9 is one week plus 2 days ahead. It copies the value 14 days before the forecast day, which is the value of day 2 of the last week: 6.

questions.q: History: 4, 6, 8, 10. What is the drift forecast for h = 2?
Baseline MAE = 20 and model MAE = 15. What is the skill score?
Your new model has MAE 9.0. The naive baseline has MAE 9.5. The data has a strong weekly season. What should you do?
options: Also test the seasonal naive baseline, which is the fair comparison
Ship the model, it beats the baseline
Remove the season from the data
why: Correct: for seasonal data the right baseline is seasonal naive. Naive is too weak here.
You compared with a weak baseline. The result is not convincing.
The season is real. Removing it hides the problem.
The mean is an even weaker baseline here.

questions.q: Why must the mean baseline be computed on the training part only?
options: Using the test data would leak future information
The test data is too small
Means are not defined for test data
why: Correct: a forecast must use only data available at the forecast time.
Size is not the issue. Leakage is.
Code length is not the reason.
A mean can always be computed. The point is whether you are allowed to use it.

questions.q: Which situation best suits the drift method?
options: A series that grows by about the same amount each step
A series with a strong weekly pattern and no trend
White noise around a fixed level
why: Correct: drift continues the average change per step.
A weekly pattern needs the seasonal naive.
Noise around a level suits the mean.
Outliers do not suit any of these baselines.
